cards.q: What is client-server architecture?
cards.a: A **client** asks for something. A **server** does the work and sends back an answer. Almost every app works like this.

cards.q: What can be a client?
cards.a: The thing the user uses, like a web browser or a mobile app. It can also be **another server**: when your server asks a payment company to charge a card, your server is the client.

cards.q: What is a server, and what work does it do?
cards.a: A computer that runs all the time and waits for requests. It checks who you are (login), reads and saves data, and follows the business rules.

cards.q: Why not do everything on the client?
cards.a: **Shared data:** everyone sees the same data, kept in one place. **Safety:** you can't trust the client. **Power:** a server can be a big, fast machine; a phone has a small battery and little memory.

cards.q: Why must important checks, like the price, happen on the server?
cards.a: **Never trust the client.** Anyone can change the app on their own phone or browser, like changing a price from 1,000 to 1. If the check happens on the server, this trick does not work.

cards.q: What happens when one server is not enough?
cards.a: One server can answer many clients at the same time. But when millions of people use the app, many servers work together. Making that work well is what system design is all about.

cards.q: What is peer-to-peer (P2P)?
cards.a: Devices talk to each other directly, with no central server. BitTorrent shares files this way. It is rare in interviews; just know that it exists.

cards.q: What do WhatsApp's ticks tell you about the client and the server?
cards.a: One grey tick: the message reached WhatsApp's server. Two grey ticks: the server delivered it to your friend's phone. Two blue ticks: your friend read it.

cards.q: What should you draw first in almost every design?
cards.a: **Client → Server → Database**. Draw this first, then improve it. And say out loud that all important checks happen on the server.

cards.q: What is the internet?
cards.a: **Many small networks joined together.** Your home Wi-Fi is a small network. Your internet company connects it to bigger networks, and those connect to the rest of the world.

cards.q: What is a packet?
cards.a: A small piece of data. Data is not sent as one big piece: it is cut into packets. A 1 MB photo becomes about 700 packets of about 1,500 bytes each.

cards.q: What does every packet carry?
cards.a: A **from** address and a **to** address, a **number** so the pieces can be put back in order, and a small **piece of the data**.

cards.q: What does a router on the internet do?
cards.a: It passes packets closer to the target, one hop at a time. Each router only knows the next stop that brings the packet closer.

cards.q: What can go wrong with packets on the way, and what fixes it?
cards.a: Packets of the same photo can take different roads, arrive **out of order**, or get **lost**. **TCP** puts them back in order and asks again for the lost ones.

cards.q: Latency vs bandwidth: what is the difference?
cards.a: **Latency** = how long one trip takes. **Bandwidth** = how much data can travel at the same time. More bandwidth doesn't lower latency, just as more lanes don't make a trip shorter.

cards.q: When does latency matter most, and when does bandwidth?
cards.a: **Latency** matters most for a web page with many small requests. **Bandwidth** matters most for a big download, like a movie.

cards.q: About how long is a round trip over different distances?
cards.a: Inside one data center: 0.5 ms. Same city: 5 ms. US East Coast ↔ Europe: 80 ms. India ↔ USA: 200 ms.

cards.q: Why do big apps run servers in many countries and use a CDN?
cards.a: **Distance adds delay.** If users are in India and servers are in the USA, every single request waits about 200 ms just for travel. Keeping data close to users makes the trip short.

cards.q: How does Netflix Open Connect make videos start faster?
cards.a: Netflix puts its own servers inside internet companies' networks. At night they copy the popular shows, so your video comes from a box near your city: a faster start and less buffering.

cards.q: What is an IP address, and what is a port?
cards.a: An **IP address** tells you which computer, like a building's address. A **port** tells you which app on that computer, like the flat number inside the building.

cards.q: What do `localhost` and `3000` mean in `http://localhost:3000`?
cards.a: `localhost` is a name that points to your own computer. Its IP address is `127.0.0.1`. `3000` is the port your app is listening on.

cards.q: IPv4 vs IPv6: what is the difference?
cards.a: **IPv4** looks like `192.168.1.10` and has only about 4.3 billion addresses, which is not enough. **IPv6** looks like `2001:db8::1`: longer, with a huge number of addresses. It is slowly replacing IPv4.

cards.q: Public IP vs private IP: what is the difference?
cards.a: A **public IP** can be reached from anywhere on the internet, like a building's street address. A **private IP** only works inside one network, like room numbers inside an office.

cards.q: How can you spot a private IP address?
cards.a: Private addresses usually start with `10.`, `172.16.` to `172.31.`, or `192.168.`.

cards.q: What is NAT?
cards.a: **Network Address Translation.** Your home router has one public IP and gives each device a private IP. When a device talks to the internet, the router swaps its private address for the public one.

cards.q: Why should only the load balancer have a public IP?
cards.a: App servers and databases stay on private IPs inside the data center, so nobody on the internet can reach your database directly. This is much safer.

cards.q: Which port numbers should you know?
cards.a: Ports go from 0 to 65535. Know **80** HTTP, **443** HTTPS, **22** SSH, **5432** PostgreSQL, **3306** MySQL, **6379** Redis and **27017** MongoDB.

cards.q: How do companies usually set up their network on AWS?
cards.a: Only the load balancer goes in a **public subnet**, the part of the network the internet can reach. App servers and databases go in **private subnets**.

cards.q: Why does AWS charge for public IPv4 addresses?
cards.a: There are not enough of them. Since February 2024, AWS charges about $3.65 a month for each one. One more reason to give a public IP only to the load balancer.

cards.q: What is DNS?
cards.a: The **Domain Name System**. It turns a **name** like `google.com` into an **IP address**. It is the contact list of the internet.

cards.q: In what order does a computer look up a website name?
cards.a: Browser cache → computer (OS) cache → DNS resolver → root server → .com server → the domain's name server. From fastest to slowest.

cards.q: What is a DNS resolver?
cards.a: The server your computer asks for the IP. It is usually run by your internet company, or is a public one like Google (`8.8.8.8`) or Cloudflare (`1.1.1.1`). If it has the answer saved, it replies right away.

cards.q: In a full DNS lookup, what do the root, .com and name servers each know?
cards.a: The **root server** knows where to find `.com`, `.org`, `.in`. The **.com server** knows which name server is in charge of `example.com`. That **name server** knows the real answer.

cards.q: Why is the full DNS lookup rare?
cards.a: The resolver **caches** the answer, so the next person gets it right away. Most lookups take just a few milliseconds.

cards.q: What is a TTL in DNS?
cards.a: **Time to live:** how long others may keep a DNS answer. `TTL = 300` means keep it for 5 minutes. Because answers are cached for the TTL, DNS changes are not instant.

cards.q: Long TTL vs short TTL: what is the tradeoff?
cards.a: **Long** (like 1 day): fewer lookups, but after an IP change some users go to the old one for up to a day. **Short** (like 1 minute): changes reach everyone quickly, but more lookups.

cards.q: What should you do with the TTL before moving your site to a new server?
cards.a: Lower the TTL a day early. Then the switch reaches everyone quickly.

cards.q: What do the DNS records A, AAAA, CNAME, MX and NS do?
cards.a: **A:** name → IPv4. **AAAA:** name → IPv6. **CNAME:** name → another name (an alias). **MX:** where to send email for the domain. **NS:** which name servers are in charge of the domain.

cards.q: What is GeoDNS?
cards.a: DNS that gives a different answer depending on where the user is, so each user goes to the nearest region. Inside each region, a load balancer spreads the traffic across servers.

cards.q: Why is DNS not enough for load balancing on its own?
cards.a: DNS can return several IPs for one name, and each client picks one. It is simple, but slow to react when a server dies, because the old answers stay cached. So we put a real load balancer behind DNS.

cards.q: Why is DNS failover to another region not instant?
cards.a: If a whole region goes down, you can point DNS to another region. But the old answers stay cached, so users don't all switch at once.

cards.q: What do the Facebook outage (2021) and the attack on Dyn (2016) teach about DNS?
cards.a: If DNS breaks, nobody can find your site, even when every server is healthy. Since the Dyn attack, many big companies use **more than one DNS provider**.

cards.q: What is anycast?
cards.a: Many servers around the world share the **same IP address**, and the internet's routers send each user to the nearest one. Cloudflare's `1.1.1.1` resolver and its CDN work this way.

cards.q: TCP vs UDP: what is the basic difference?
cards.a: **TCP** is like a tracked courier: safe and in order, but a little slower. **UDP** is like throwing flyers from a moving car: very fast, but nobody checks if each one arrived.

cards.q: What four promises does TCP make?
cards.a: Every packet arrives (lost ones are sent again), packets arrive in order, there are no duplicates, and it slows down when the network is busy.

cards.q: How does the TCP handshake work?
cards.a: Three short messages open the connection before any data moves: **SYN** (can we talk?), **SYN-ACK** (yes, can you hear me?), **ACK** (yes!).

cards.q: Why do apps reuse open TCP connections?
cards.a: The handshake costs **one full round trip** before any data is sent. From India to a server in the USA, that is about 200 ms of waiting.

cards.q: How does TCP fix lost packets?
cards.a: The receiver sends back an **ACK** (acknowledgment) for what it got. If a packet goes missing, the sender notices and sends it again.

cards.q: What does UDP skip, and what do you gain?
cards.a: No handshake, no resending (a lost packet is gone), and no ordering. Less work means **less delay**. The app decides what to do about lost packets, and often the answer is nothing.

cards.q: When should you pick UDP instead of TCP?
cards.a: **Use TCP by default.** Pick UDP only when old data is useless: voice and video calls, and online games, where a late update is worse than a missing one.

cards.q: Why do video calls use UDP?
cards.a: A frame from one second ago doesn't matter anymore, so skip it and show the next one. A tiny glitch, like a short robot voice, is better than a frozen screen.

cards.q: Why is streaming video, even a live stream, not a UDP case?
cards.a: The video is sent as small chunks over normal HTTP, through a CDN. The player keeps a few seconds of video ready, so a resent packet is never noticed.

cards.q: What is QUIC?
cards.a: A protocol Google created. It runs on **UDP** and adds TCP's safety on top, but sets up connections faster and works better on phones. **HTTP/3** uses QUIC.

cards.q: Which things run on TCP, and why?
cards.a: Web pages, APIs, chat messages, payments and database connections, because every piece must arrive, in order. Everything that uses HTTP already runs on TCP (or QUIC).

cards.q: What is HTTP?
cards.a: The language browsers and servers use to talk. The browser sends a **request**, and the server sends back a **response**.

cards.q: What are the parts of an HTTP request and an HTTP response?
cards.a: **Request:** method + path, headers, body. **Response:** status code, headers, body. Headers are extra notes, like the format or how long to cache.

cards.q: What does it mean that HTTP is stateless?
cards.a: The server forgets you after every request. That is why the browser sends a **cookie** or a **token** with every single request.

cards.q: What is HTTPS?
cards.a: **HTTP + TLS:** HTTP inside a locked box. Only your browser and the server can open it. Nobody in the middle, like the café Wi-Fi owner or your internet company, can read or change it.

cards.q: What three things does TLS give you?
cards.a: **Privacy:** nobody can read the data. **No tampering:** nobody can change it on the way. **The right server:** you are really talking to `bank.com`, checked with a certificate.

cards.q: How does the TLS handshake create a secret key?
cards.a: The browser sends its half of a key. The server sends its certificate and its half. The browser checks the certificate, then both combine the halves into the same secret key. The key itself is never sent.

cards.q: Why does a new HTTPS connection wait about two round trips?
cards.a: One round trip for the TCP handshake, plus one more for the TLS handshake, before any data moves. Another reason to **reuse connections**.

cards.q: What is a certificate in HTTPS?
cards.a: The server's ID card. It says "this key belongs to `bank.com`". It is signed by a **Certificate Authority (CA)**, a company browsers trust, like Let's Encrypt or DigiCert.

cards.q: What happens if a certificate is fake, for the wrong site, or expired?
cards.a: The browser shows a big warning page. Certificates expire after a few months, so they must be renewed. Good teams renew them automatically.

cards.q: What is TLS termination?
cards.a: HTTPS ends at the **load balancer**. It decrypts the request and passes it to the app servers over the private network. Many companies now encrypt the inside traffic too, especially for sensitive data (**zero trust**).

cards.q: Why end TLS at the load balancer?
cards.a: Certificates live in one place, app servers don't spend CPU on encryption, and the load balancer can read the request to send `/api` and `/images` to different servers.

cards.q: HTTP/1.1 vs HTTP/2 vs HTTP/3: what changed?
cards.a: **HTTP/1.1:** one request at a time on each connection. **HTTP/2:** many requests at the same time on one connection. **HTTP/3:** runs on QUIC (UDP), so one lost packet doesn't make everything else wait.

cards.q: What did Firesheep (2010) show about HTTPS?
cards.a: On café Wi-Fi, anyone could take over other people's Facebook and Twitter accounts with one click, because those sites didn't use HTTPS for everything. After that, big sites moved to HTTPS for every page.

cards.q: How do HTTP, TLS and TCP fit together in HTTPS?
cards.a: In layers. **HTTP** writes the message, **TLS** (under HTTP) locks it, and **TCP** (under TLS) carries it. HTTP/3 swaps TCP for QUIC, which runs on UDP.

cards.q: What does each HTTP method do?
cards.a: `GET` read, `POST` create, `PUT` replace the whole thing, `PATCH` change a part, `DELETE` remove.

cards.q: `PUT` vs `PATCH`: what is the difference?
cards.a: `PUT` replaces the whole thing, like user 7's full profile. `PATCH` changes only a part, like just the delivery address of an order.

cards.q: What do "safe" and "idempotent" mean for an HTTP method?
cards.a: **Safe:** it changes nothing. **Idempotent:** doing it once or many times gives the same result.

cards.q: Which HTTP methods are safe, and which are idempotent?
cards.a: Of the five main methods, only `GET` is safe (`HEAD` and `OPTIONS` are safe too). `GET`, `PUT` and `DELETE` are idempotent. `PATCH` is not always idempotent, and `POST` is not.

cards.q: What goes wrong if an app retries `POST /orders` after the reply was lost?
cards.a: The first order was already created, so the retry creates a second one, and the user can be charged twice. `POST` is not idempotent.

cards.q: How does an idempotency key make a retry safe?
cards.a: The app sends a unique key, like `Idempotency-Key: 7f3a9c`. The server remembers it. If the same key comes again, it sends back the first result instead of creating a new order.

cards.q: What do the status code groups 2xx, 3xx, 4xx and 5xx mean?
cards.a: **2xx:** success. **3xx:** go somewhere else. **4xx:** client mistake. **5xx:** server problem.

cards.q: `401` vs `403`: what is the difference?
cards.a: `401` Unauthorized: you are not logged in ("Who are you?"). `403` Forbidden: you are logged in, but not allowed ("I know who you are, but no").

cards.q: When do you return `201`, `204` and `409`?
cards.a: `201` Created: a new thing was created (after `POST`). `204` No Content: it worked, with nothing to send back (after `DELETE`). `409` Conflict: it clashes with something, like a username that is taken.

cards.q: What do `429` and `503` mean?
cards.a: `429` Too Many Requests: slow down, you hit a rate limit. `503` Service Unavailable: the server is overloaded or down for maintenance.

cards.q: `500` vs `502` vs `504`: what is the difference?
cards.a: `500`: a bug on the server. `502` Bad Gateway: the load balancer got a broken answer from the server behind it. `504` Gateway Timeout: the server behind the load balancer took too long.

cards.q: `301` vs `302`: what is the difference?
cards.a: `301` Moved Permanently: the address changed forever. `302` Found: go to this other address for now.

cards.q: When should a client retry a failed request?
cards.a: On `5xx`, `429` or no answer, but only if the request is safe to repeat: `GET`, `PUT`, `DELETE`, or a `POST` with an idempotency key. Don't retry other `4xx`: fix the request first.

cards.q: How long should a client wait before it retries?
cards.a: Wait longer each time (**backoff**), plus a little random extra time (**jitter**), so thousands of clients don't all retry at the same moment. If the server sends `Retry-After`, wait that long.

cards.q: What do the headers `Content-Type`, `Authorization`, `Cache-Control` and `Location` do?
cards.a: `Content-Type`: the format of the body. `Authorization`: who you are. `Cache-Control`: how long the response may be cached. `Location`: where to go, or where the new thing is.

cards.q: How do `ETag` and `304 Not Modified` save time and data?
cards.a: The server sends a version tag (`ETag`). Later the browser asks again with `If-None-Match`. If nothing changed, the server answers `304` and sends no body.

cards.q: What is an API?
cards.a: The menu of your system. It lists what other programs can ask for, and how to ask.

cards.q: What are the three rules of REST?
cards.a: Everything is a **resource** (a thing, like an order). Each resource has its own **URL**, like `/orders/42`. **HTTP methods** say what you want to do with it.

cards.q: Why should REST URLs use nouns, not verbs?
cards.a: The HTTP method is already the verb. Use `POST /orders`, not `POST /createOrder`, and `DELETE /orders/42`, not `POST /orders/42/delete`.

cards.q: How should you name resources in REST URLs?
cards.a: Plural nouns, lowercase, with hyphens: `/orders` for the list, `/orders/42` for one order, and `/menu-items`, not `/Menu_Items`. A thing each user has only one of, like `/cart`, stays singular.

cards.q: When should you nest REST URLs?
cards.a: Only for "belongs to": `/restaurants/17/menu-items` means the menu items of restaurant 17. Don't go deeper than one or two levels.

cards.q: Where do filters and sorting go in a REST API?
cards.a: In the query string, like `GET /restaurants?city=pune&sort=rating&limit=20`.

cards.q: How should a REST API return an error?
cards.a: With a real error code **and** a clear error body, like `409` with an `error` code and a `message`. The `error` code is for programs. The `message` is for people.

cards.q: How do you design a small REST API, step by step?
cards.a: List the features. Find the nouns: they become resources. Write **one endpoint per feature**, so you can check every feature is covered. Pick the method and success code. Take the user from the login token.

cards.q: Why take the user from the login token, never from the request body?
cards.a: Otherwise anyone could place orders as someone else.

cards.q: What are common mistakes in REST APIs?
cards.a: Verbs in URLs, the user ID taken from the body instead of the token, `200 OK` with an error message inside, a list of 100,000 items with no paging, and breaking old apps without a new version.

cards.q: What should a REST API do with big lists and with changes?
cards.a: Send big lists in **pages**. Give the API a new **version** when it changes, so old apps don't break.

cards.q: What body format and caching does a REST API normally use?
cards.a: **JSON** is the normal format for bodies. `GET` responses can be cached with the `Cache-Control` header.

cards.q: How does Stripe change its API without breaking old apps?
cards.a: `/v1` has stayed in the URL for years. Real changes get **date-named versions**, like `2024-06-20`. Each account stays on its version until it upgrades, and an app can ask for one with the `Stripe-Version` header.

cards.q: What is RPC?
cards.a: **Remote Procedure Call:** you call a function, but it runs on another server. REST style is `GET /users/7`. RPC style is `getUser(7)`.

cards.q: How does gRPC work?
cards.a: You write a contract in a `.proto` file. A tool generates code from it for many languages. Data travels as **Protocol Buffers**, and it runs on **HTTP/2**, so many calls share one connection.

cards.q: What are Protocol Buffers?
cards.a: The compact **binary** format gRPC uses to send data. It is smaller and faster to read than JSON.

cards.q: What are the good and bad sides of gRPC?
cards.a: **Good:** very fast, and both sides must follow the same contract, so mistakes show up early. **Bad:** browsers can't call it directly (you need **gRPC-Web**, usually with a proxy like Envoy in between), and binary data is hard to read when you debug.

cards.q: Where does gRPC usually sit in a system?
cards.a: **Inside**, between your own services: the API gateway calls the services with gRPC, and the services call each other with it. Apps and browsers talk REST or GraphQL (JSON) to the gateway at the front door.

cards.q: What is GraphQL?
cards.a: A way for the client to ask for **exactly the data it needs** in one query, and get it back in exactly that shape.

cards.q: What are over-fetching and under-fetching?
cards.a: **Over-fetching:** getting more than you need, like 30 fields when you need only the name. **Under-fetching:** one request is not enough, so you need many round trips.

cards.q: How does GraphQL work behind the scenes?
cards.a: There is usually one endpoint, `POST /graphql`. A **schema** describes every type and field the client may ask for. Small functions called **resolvers** fetch each field, often from different services.

cards.q: What are the good sides of GraphQL?
cards.a: No over-fetching, fewer round trips, and each screen can ask for different data without new endpoints.

cards.q: What are the downsides of GraphQL?
cards.a: **Caching is harder**, because every request is a `POST` to the same URL. A client can send a **very expensive query**, so you need limits on depth and cost. And resolvers can cause the N+1 problem.

cards.q: What is the N+1 problem in GraphQL, and how do you fix it?
cards.a: Resolvers can cause many small database calls. The fix is to **batch** them.

cards.q: When do you pick REST, gRPC or GraphQL?
cards.a: **REST** by default. **gRPC** for busy service-to-service calls inside your system. **GraphQL** when many different clients and screens need different shapes of data.

cards.q: Where did gRPC and GraphQL come from?
cards.a: **gRPC** came from Google, which released it in 2015. **GraphQL** came from Facebook, which built it in 2012 for its mobile News Feed and made it open source in 2015.

cards.q: Why do apps need polling, SSE or WebSockets?
cards.a: With normal HTTP, the client asks and the server answers. The server can never start the conversation. But many apps need updates as soon as they happen, like a new chat message.

cards.q: What is polling?
cards.a: The client asks every few seconds: "Anything new?" It is the simplest option and works everywhere.

cards.q: What is wrong with polling?
cards.a: Most answers are "no", so most requests are wasted, and news can be late by up to the polling gap. 1 million users polling every 5 seconds is **200,000 requests per second**.

cards.q: What is long polling?
cards.a: The client asks, and the server **holds the request open** until there is news, or until a timeout (like 30 seconds). Then the client asks again right away.

cards.q: What are the good and bad sides of long polling?
cards.a: **Good:** almost instant, and still plain HTTP. **Bad:** the server holds many open requests, and every update needs a brand-new request.

cards.q: What is SSE (Server-Sent Events)?
cards.a: One HTTP connection that stays open, and the server sends events down it whenever it wants. Data flows **one way only**: server to client. Browsers reconnect by themselves if it drops.

cards.q: What is SSE good for?
cards.a: Notifications, live scores, stock prices, and AI answers that appear word by word. OpenAI's API streams its answers over SSE.

cards.q: How does a WebSocket connection start?
cards.a: As a normal HTTP request with the header `Upgrade: websocket`. The server answers `101 Switching Protocols`, and the connection becomes a **two-way channel** that stays open.

cards.q: What are WebSockets good for?
cards.a: Truly real-time messages in **both directions**, with very little extra data per message: chat, games and editing together. Slack keeps a WebSocket open, so new messages arrive instantly.

cards.q: Why are WebSockets harder to scale?
cards.a: Each server holds many open connections, and you must know **which server holds which user**.

cards.q: How do you choose between polling, SSE and WebSockets?
cards.a: A few seconds of delay is okay: **polling**. Mostly the server sends: **SSE**. Both sides talk: **WebSockets**. Pick the simplest option that is fast enough.

cards.q: How does a chat message reach a user connected to a different chat server?
cards.a: With **pub/sub**, like Redis Pub/Sub. Server 1 publishes the message on Ben's channel. Server 2, which holds Ben's connection, is subscribed to it, gets the message, and pushes it down Ben's WebSocket.

cards.q: What else must you plan for when servers hold open connections?
cards.a: The **load balancer** must support long-lived connections. And when a server restarts, its users get disconnected, so clients must **reconnect automatically**.

cards.q: Why do open connections need a heartbeat?
cards.a: Load balancers and proxies close a connection that stays quiet too long (often after about 60 seconds). A tiny ping every 30 seconds or so keeps it open, and shows quickly when the other side is gone.

cards.q: Why can SSE run into trouble over HTTP/1.1?
cards.a: A browser opens only about 6 connections per site, and each SSE stream keeps one busy. With many tabs open, the site can run out. Over HTTP/2, many streams share one connection.

cards.q: What is a cookie?
cards.a: A small piece of data (up to about 4 KB) that a server asks the browser to keep, with `Set-Cookie`. The browser then sends it back **automatically**, in a `Cookie` header, on every request to that site.

cards.q: What do the cookie flags `HttpOnly`, `Secure` and `SameSite` do?
cards.a: `HttpOnly`: JavaScript can't read it, so a malicious script can't steal it. `Secure`: only sent over HTTPS. `SameSite`: limits sending it on requests another site starts (CSRF). `Strict`: never. `Lax`: only when the user clicks a link to the site. `None`: always.

cards.q: How does a login session work?
cards.a: The server creates a session record (like session `abc123` = user 7) and stores it in a session store, usually Redis. You get only the session ID, in a cookie. On every request, the server looks up that ID.

cards.q: Why keep sessions in Redis instead of inside one app server?
cards.a: Then **any** server can handle **any** request, and the app servers stay stateless.

cards.q: What are the good and bad sides of sessions?
cards.a: **Good:** logging out is easy. Delete the session, and the user is logged out at once, on every server (delete all their sessions to log out every device). **Bad:** every request needs a lookup in the session store.

cards.q: What is a JWT made of?
cards.a: Three parts joined by dots: **header.payload.signature**. The payload is just encoded JSON, like the user ID, the role and the expiry time (`exp`).

cards.q: How does a server check a JWT?
cards.a: It checks the **signature** and the expiry time (`exp`), with **no database lookup**. If anyone changes even one letter of the payload, the signature stops matching, and the token is rejected.

cards.q: Why must you never put secrets in a JWT?
cards.a: A JWT is **signed, not encrypted**. Anyone can read the payload.

cards.q: Why sign JWTs with a private key (`RS256`) instead of one shared secret (`HS256`)?
cards.a: Only the auth service has the private key. Other services check tokens with the public key, which can check them but not make them. With a shared secret, every service that checks tokens could also make fake ones.

cards.q: Where should a JWT be kept in a browser?
cards.a: In an `HttpOnly` cookie. A token that JavaScript can read can be stolen by a malicious script. Mobile apps and other services send it in the `Authorization: Bearer` header instead.

cards.q: What is the big problem with JWTs, and the usual fix?
cards.a: You can't easily take one back: it stays valid until it expires. The fix is a short-lived **access token** (like 15 minutes) plus a longer-lived **refresh token**.

cards.q: What is a refresh token used for?
cards.a: Only to get a new access token. It lives longer, it can be cancelled on the server, and it should be replaced each time it is used.

cards.q: Sessions vs JWT: when do you use which?
cards.a: A normal website with one backend: **sessions in a cookie**. Many services, mobile apps or "log in with" flows: **short JWTs + refresh tokens**.

cards.q: What did the "alg: none" JWT bug (2015) teach?
cards.a: Some libraries accepted tokens that said no signature was needed, so attackers could write any payload. Always check the signature with the algorithm **you** expect, never the one the token asks for.

cards.q: What did Facebook's "View As" bug (2018) teach about tokens?
cards.a: Attackers stole access tokens and could act as users without a password. Facebook cancelled the tokens of about 90 million accounts. Tokens are keys: if they leak, you must be able to cancel them.

cards.q: What is a proxy?
cards.a: A server that sits **in the middle** and passes messages on someone else's behalf.

cards.q: Forward proxy vs reverse proxy: who does each one work for?
cards.a: A **forward proxy** works for the **clients**, like an office receptionist making outside calls. A **reverse proxy** works for the **servers**, like a hotel front desk.

cards.q: What is a forward proxy used for?
cards.a: Company rules (block and log websites), privacy (websites see the proxy's IP, not yours), shared caching (fetch a file once for many people), and getting around blocks in your region.

cards.q: What jobs does a reverse proxy do?
cards.a: Load balancing, HTTPS (it holds the certificate), caching, compression, security (it hides the real servers and blocks bad traffic), and routing.

cards.q: What does each kind of proxy hide?
cards.a: A **forward proxy** hides who the client is. A **reverse proxy** hides which servers are behind it.

cards.q: Who sets up a forward proxy, and who sets up a reverse proxy?
cards.a: A forward proxy is set up by the client side: a company, a school or a user. A reverse proxy is set up by the website owner.

cards.q: How does a reverse proxy route requests?
cards.a: By path. It sends `/api` to the API servers and `/images` to the image servers. In Nginx, a `location /api/` block with `proxy_pass` does this.

cards.q: Reverse proxy vs load balancer vs API gateway: how do they relate?
cards.a: A **reverse proxy** is the general idea: a middleman for servers. A **load balancer** is one whose main job is spreading traffic. An **API gateway** adds API features: login checks, rate limits, API keys.

cards.q: What are some examples of reverse proxies and forward proxies?
cards.a: **Reverse:** Nginx, HAProxy, Envoy, Cloudflare. **Forward:** office web filters, Squid. In real systems, one tool like Nginx or Envoy often does the jobs of reverse proxy, load balancer and API gateway.

cards.q: How does Cloudflare work as a giant reverse proxy?
cards.a: Your browser actually connects to Cloudflare's servers. Cloudflare blocks attacks, serves cached files, and passes the rest to the site's real servers, which stay hidden.

cards.q: What are the main steps when you type a URL and press Enter?
cards.a: Read the URL and check the browser cache → **DNS** finds the IP → **TCP** handshake → **TLS** handshake → **HTTP request** with the cookie → CDN / load balancer → app server → cache / database → **response** → the browser builds the page, with more requests for CSS, JS and images.

cards.q: What do the parts of `https://shop.example.com/products/42` tell the browser?
cards.a: **Scheme** `https`: how to talk, HTTP inside TLS, on port 443 by default. **Host** `shop.example.com`: which server, found with DNS. **Path** `/products/42`: what you want on that server.

cards.q: How can a page, image or script load with no network request at all?
cards.a: The browser checks its own cache first. If `Cache-Control` from the last visit says the saved copy is still fresh, it uses it. HTML is usually kept only briefly, but images, CSS and JavaScript often come straight from the cache.

cards.q: When a request reaches a website, which machines does it pass through?
cards.a: A **CDN edge** answers if it has a copy. If not, a **load balancer** picks a healthy **app server**. The app server reads the cookie to find out who you are, checks the **cache** first, and goes to the **database** only on a cache miss.

cards.q: About how long before the first byte, for a new HTTPS connection from India to a server in the USA?
cards.a: Three round trips of about 200 ms: the TCP handshake, the TLS 1.3 handshake, then request + response. So about **600 ms plus server time**, and more if DNS was not cached. Most of the wait is travel, not the server.

cards.q: How does a nearby CDN edge server cut the wait for a user in India?
cards.a: The handshakes become short trips, about 10 ms each. If the edge has a copy, it all takes about 30 ms. If not, the edge reuses its open connection to the origin, so only **one** long trip is left: about 280 ms instead of 650 ms.

cards.q: How many round trips does the TLS handshake cost in TLS 1.3, and in TLS 1.2?
cards.a: **TLS 1.3:** one round trip. **TLS 1.2:** two. TLS 1.3, finished in 2018, removed a whole round trip from every new HTTPS connection.

cards.q: How does HTTP/3 make a new connection faster?
cards.a: It runs on QUIC, which does the connection setup and the TLS handshake **together, in one round trip**. So a new connection needs 2 round trips before the first byte instead of 3: about 450 ms instead of 650 ms from India to the USA.

cards.q: After the HTML arrives, how does the browser load the rest of the page?
cards.a: It finds links to CSS, JavaScript and images, and asks for them on the **connection that is already open**, many at once with HTTP/2. Then it draws the page, and the JavaScript calls APIs, like `GET /api/cart`, to fill in personal data.

cards.q: How should you answer "What happens when you type a URL?" in an interview?
cards.a: Go through **every step briefly, in order**: cache, DNS, TCP, TLS, request, servers, response, page. Give the round-trip numbers. Then ask the interviewer which part to go deeper on.

cards.q: From India to a server in the USA, how much does reusing an open connection save?
cards.a: A second request on the same connection skips the TCP and TLS handshakes. It costs one round trip plus server time: about **250 ms** instead of about **650 ms** on a new connection.

cards.q: Why send a personal page with `Cache-Control: private, no-cache` and an `ETag`?
cards.a: `private`: only the browser may keep it, never a CDN, so no one else gets your page. `no-cache`: the browser must ask first. It sends the `ETag` back, and if nothing changed, the server answers `304 Not Modified` with no body.
